extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students / beginning proof writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and techniques for composing clear, correct mathematical proofs, including general writing rules (notation, grammar, audience) and common proof methods (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, cases, constructive/existential, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish notation and recall assumptions at start
rubrics_metrics.description: All written proofs should begin by establishing notation and recalling assumptions. We may also recall a definition if it is used within a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State initial assumptions and any definitions you will use so the reader knows the context for subsequent steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify every non-widely-known claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Each new mathematical claim that is not well known should be justified by reasoning or a reputable reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either provide the reasoning for a claim or cite a reputable source (lecture notes, textbook) to back it up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the audience as one’s peers
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience for a written proof should be considered to be a group of one’s peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write at the level of your classmates: neither overly hand-holding nor skipping nontrivial steps without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare your method of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: It is customary to declare your method of proof in order to inform the reader (e.g. 'For the sake of contradiction, we assume that...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state 'By induction', 'By contradiction', 'We prove the contrapositive', etc., so the reader knows the overall plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define each new symbol when introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: Always define a new symbol: 'Let x denote a natural number...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce and define any variable or notation the first time it appears to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reuse the same letter for different meanings within a proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Never reuse the same letter for a different meaning in the same proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reusing letters for different objects in one proof is confusing and error-prone; pick distinct symbols for distinct roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redefine symbols if reused after proof completion
rubrics_metrics.description: We may reuse a letter after a proof is complete, but it should always be redefined in its new context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you use variable names later in a different proof or section, explicitly redefine them for the new context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof must read as a logical sequence of steps
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof must read as a logical sequence of steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each line follows logically from previous lines, definitions, or cited results; avoid unjustified leaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof should make sense when read aloud in English
rubrics_metrics.description: It must make sense in English when read out aloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose sentences so that the argument is intelligible in full-sentence form, not only as symbolic manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance words and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should read as a balance of words and symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use words to explain the intent and structure, and symbols for precise statements—don't rely solely on dense symbolic lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain grammatical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof must be grammatically correct in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good grammar aids clarity; sentence fragments and poor punctuation can obscure logical structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not begin a sentence with a mathematical symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not begin a sentence with a mathematical symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead sentences with words; if a symbolic statement is needed, embed it in a grammatically complete sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly state the status of each mathematical statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The status of each mathematical statement should be explicitly declared: 'We assume that...', 'We must show that...', 'We conclude that...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label assumptions, goals, intermediate claims, and conclusions so the reader can follow the argument's structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantifiers to indicate truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifiers should be used to indicate the truth of a statement: 'For all x in Z we have...', 'There exists x in Z satisfying...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about domains and quantification to avoid ambiguity (e.g., 'for all x ∈ A' vs. 'there exists x').

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite earlier theorems and reputable sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Any method of proof may use earlier theorems. They should be cited by a reputable source (e.g., lecture notes or other class material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking known results, name or reference them so the reader can verify their applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate when the proof is complete
rubrics_metrics.description: Inform the reader when the proof is complete: 'This completes the proof.' Or use QED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End proofs with an explicit closing statement or symbol so the reader knows the argument has finished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer shorter, simpler, clearer proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: One method is generally preferred over another if it is shorter, simpler or clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple valid proofs exist, choose the one that communicates the idea most efficiently and understandably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect trial and error and creative steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs are often arrived at by trial and error, writing and revision; they may involve a 'creative step' or 'new idea'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft, revise, and be prepared to try different approaches; clarity often emerges after reworking the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct proof establishes the result using direct arguments and deductions that are natural consequences of the definitions and assumptions. For 'If P then Q', begin by assuming P and deduce Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use definitions, assumptions, and logical equivalences in a chain that leads from P to Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive method
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove the contrapositive: (not Q) => (not P), since 'P implies Q' is equivalent to its contrapositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is often easier when Q is a compound statement (e.g., P => (Q ∧ R) or P => (Q ∨ R)); use the appropriate contrapositive forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove Q under assumptions A, suppose A is true but Q is false and derive a contradiction; for P => Q, assume P and not Q and obtain a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that assumptions plus the negation of the conclusion lead to an inconsistency (a statement and its opposite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'sketch proof' is an intuitive outline of a proof giving an overview of the main ideas when full details are beyond scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sketch proofs to convey the main ideas—explicitly note omitted details or indicate where a full proof can be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving bi-conditional statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove P ⇔ Q it is necessary to prove both implications P => Q and Q => P; proving only one is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the proof you may use any method for each implication; treat each direction independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disprove by counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: A counterexample is an exception to a proposed general rule; a single counterexample suffices to show the rule is false in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To disprove a universal claim, exhibit a concrete example in the claimed domain where the statement fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting statements that have counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement with counterexamples can often be repaired by restricting the universe of values or restricting the conclusion to make a true statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a counterexample is found, consider weakening the claim or narrowing the domain to salvage a correct theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof can be carried out by breaking possibilities into several cases and writing a separate proof for each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose natural, exhaustive cases (e.g., n ∈ Z: n even or n odd; n < 0 or n ≥ 0) and verify the statement in each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive existence proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructive proof demonstrates existence by explicitly constructing an element x in a set A and showing it satisfies the required property P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the explicit construction and verify the required properties to establish existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential (nonconstructive) proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: An existential proof establishes the existence of an element with certain properties without constructing it explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that such an element must exist (e.g., by pigeonhole principle, indirect argument) even if no explicit example is given.
